newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Premier tries to defuse ethnic tension in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Premier tries to defuse ethnic tension in Zaire.

text.p: Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo tried on Wednesday to ease ethnic tension following an army crackdown on Tutsis in the east of the country.
Kengo told a news conference South Kivu Province deputy governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabandji overstepped his powers by ordering some 200,000 Banyamulenge Tutsis to leave.
"The deputy governor overstepped his mark in declaring war in the east. He has been suspended as a result," Kengo said.
But Kengo's intervention a full week after the quit order pushed up tension in the region may have come too late.

Aid workers in the east reported that Zairean soldiers embroiled in fighting with the Banyamulenge had launched an operation against Tutsis on the plateau above the town of Uvira. No details were immediately available.
The Banyamulenge Tutsis immigrated from Rwanda about 200 years ago but have been locked in clashes with indigenous Zaireans who resent their relative wealth.

Lwabandji insisted on Tuesday that Banyamulenge villagers on the plateau, where armed Tutsis have their strongholds, must come down and surrender. Those who did not "would be treated as rebels and exterminated", he told Reuters.
Lwabandji said then he had been reinstated by the central government that declared him suspended for his order.
Kengo said only the president and parliament could declare war or a state of emergency.
The prime minister said regional authorities were "resorting to passion" in trying to resolve the conflict between Banyamulenge and indigenous Zaireans.
At the same time he accused neighbouring Rwanda, whose government and army are dominated by Tutsis, of arming the Banyamulenge.
"We have enough proof that they (Banyamulenge) are not alone. They are being helped by Rwanda which is providing them with heavy weapons," he said.
Kengo said diplomatic efforts between the two countries were vital to prevent fighting from engulfing the entire Great Lakes region of Central Africa, which also includes Burundi.
Like Rwanda, the army and regime in Burundi are controlled by Tutsis and the plight of the Banyamulenge risks drawing troops of the two countries into a wider conflict.
Zairean and Rwandan troops have exchanged heavy fire in the border area around the South Kivu provincial capital Bukavu.
The conflict has degenerated into virtual civil war since more than a million Hutus, historic enmies of the Tutsi, fled violence in Rwanda into the same region in 1994.
Hutus are blamed for the genocide of up to a million Tutsis or their Hutu sympathisers in Rwanda at that time.
